Running the settlement programme: frequency, field survey practice and the NDE that follows

Short answer: API 653 does not give one calendar frequency for settlement surveys. Annex B says surveys during operation should follow a planned frequency, based on predicted soil settlement or, for older tanks with no baseline, on service history. A full settlement survey is mandatory around a hydrostatic test, unless the tank's history shows settlement is acceptable and none is expected. Inch-scale movement across two cycles counts as active settlement. That calls for a shorter, trend-based survey interval set by the owner and the authorized inspector, plus an engineer's projection to the next inspection date.

The sections above explain how to break a survey into its Annex B components and judge each one. This section covers the practical side: survey frequency, repeatable data, ringwall behaviour, the NDE that follows, and who decides. It paraphrases API Std 653. Check limits and clause numbers against your licensed copy of the current edition.

Check the edition first: Addendum 4 (July 2025)

The source note near the top of this article lists API 653, 5th edition, with Addenda 1 through 3. API has since issued Addendum 4 (July 2025), which revised the text on tank-bottom thickness measurement. The Annex B settlement method is still the framework, but before you sign an evaluation, confirm the edition and addendum your inspection programme follows, and check whether your jurisdiction or contract fixes a specific edition. For example, federal pipeline rules incorporate a dated edition by reference. API's own standards pages are the place to confirm what is current. Do not rely on an older edition copied online. Those copies are often decades out of date.

How often to survey: build the frequency, don't look it up

Annex B treats survey frequency as engineering planning, not a fixed interval. Predicted settlement depends on soil type, fill history, foundation design and tank age, and the owner is expected to set the frequency from those factors. The 2003 edition, which is publicly available because federal regulation incorporates it, already said this. It also said that tanks with no baseline data should be monitored on the basis of their prior service history. Later editions kept that approach.

In practice, most owners combine planned surveys with surveys triggered by events. A defensible plan usually includes the following triggers, each with a reason recorded in the tank file:

TriggerSurvey normally takenWhy it matters
Hydrostatic test after repair, alteration or reconstructionShell elevation survey before filling, during filling and at full test levelAPI 653 requires settlement measurement during a hydrotest unless a documented history shows acceptable settlement with none expected
Out-of-service internal inspectionInternal bottom elevation survey plus edge breakover measurementsThis is the only time bottom depressions, bulges and edge settlement can be measured directly
Routine in-service or external inspection finds signs of movementShell elevation survey at the established pointsThe visual signs are shell-to-foundation gaps, ringwall cracking, water ponding at the chime, or binding on a floating-roof seal
Measured rate is accelerating between surveysShorter survey interval set by the owner, with a projection to the next due dateAnnex B allows edge settlement to be compared against the limit as measured only when little further movement is expected
Site eventsSurvey after the eventFlooding, pad erosion, nearby excavation or piling, a major leak that saturates the subgrade, or seismic activity
Service change to heavier product or higher fill heightBaseline survey before the change and a follow-up after the first full cyclesA higher foundation load changes the settlement prediction that the original frequency was based on
Foundation repair or re-levelingNew baseline surveyThe earlier trend no longer describes the current geometry

The reader's case, roughly one inch of differential settlement over two inspection cycles on a ringwall, falls on the "accelerating" row. The useful figure is the rate at each survey point, not the total. Divide each point's change by the time between surveys. Then ask the engineer to project the uniform, tilt, out-of-plane and edge components to the next planned inspection, and set the next survey date so that a limit cannot be crossed unseen. Inch-per-cycle movement is often surveyed annually until two consecutive surveys show the rate is falling. That is an owner decision and should be recorded as one. It is not a code number.

Ringwall foundations: what an inch means on concrete

A reinforced concrete ringwall carries the shell on a stiff, narrow footing, while the bottom plate rests on compacted fill inside it. The two parts can settle differently, and the pattern of movement shows which part is moving.

  • The ringwall itself moves. If soil beneath the ringwall varies around the circumference, the shell elevations show tilt and out-of-plane settlement. This is the shell survey covered earlier in this article. Look for cracked or rotated ringwall segments at the low points, and for a gap opening between the bottom plate and the top of the ringwall.
  • The fill inside the ringwall consolidates. The bottom drops relative to the shell, and the breakover forms just inside the ringwall. Annex B assesses this as edge settlement, and the shell survey can show almost nothing while the floor is already near its limit. This is the most common reason an "acceptable" shell survey and a failing internal inspection both turn up on the same tank.
  • Water gets in at the chime. When the seal between the bottom plate projection and the ringwall cracks, or the ringwall top rotates away from the plate, rainwater can run under the bottom. That drives soil-side corrosion of the floor near the shell, where the code's bottom thickness limits are tightest and where edge settlement already concentrates strain. Settlement and underside corrosion often show up together on ringwall tanks, so they should be evaluated together.

The ringwall levelness tolerance quoted earlier applies to new or reconstructed foundations. It is not an in-service acceptance limit.

Collecting survey data that can be compared cycle to cycle

A trend is only meaningful if each survey is repeatable. Annex B asks for experienced personnel, equipment accurate enough to resolve the differences being measured, and the same points reused in later surveys. In field terms, that means:

  • A stable benchmark away from the tank and its foundation. A benchmark on the ringwall or a nearby support moves with the tank and hides the uniform component.
  • Permanent, marked survey points. Use points that can be found again, such as paint-marked or stamped locations on the shell, or the course-one-to-course-two weld where the bottom projection is distorted. Number them in the same direction every time.
  • A recorded product level and temperature. Settlement under load is partly elastic. Comparing a survey at a high fill level with one at a low fill level adds a load-dependent difference that is not settlement. Survey at a consistent fill level, or at least record the level so the engineer can account for it.
  • Closure of the level loop. Close the survey back onto the benchmark and record the closure error. If the closure error is close to the out-of-plane value being judged, the survey cannot support the evaluation.
  • The method and instrument recorded. Digital levels, total stations and 3D laser scanning all produce elevation data, each with its own precision. Use the same method for the Annex B points every cycle.
  • Repeatable internal bottom grids. When the tank is out of service, survey along fixed diametrical lines and mark the edges of depressions.

For shell geometry beyond elevation, such as roundness, verticality and local shell distortion near low points, see our tank 3D scanning page, which explains what a scan captures that a level loop does not.

Hydrotest settlement monitoring

API 653 makes a settlement survey mandatory for an existing tank that undergoes a hydrostatic test. The only exception is a tank with documented service history showing acceptable settlement, where none is expected during the test. Settlement is measured during filling and when the water reaches the full test level, using the same point count and spacing rules discussed earlier in this article.

Owners usually set hold points before filling, with limits fixed in advance by the engineer. If movement is unexpected, the owner's engineer and the authorized inspector decide whether to continue, and the survey team reports readings promptly. Keep the hydrotest survey as the new baseline.

The NDE a settlement finding should trigger

Annex B links settlement directly to weld examination. Where edge settlement passes a fraction of its allowable, shell-to-bottom and nearby bottom welds are to be examined visually and by magnetic particle or liquid penetrant methods, and any indications repaired or evaluated, as described earlier in this article. Beyond that code-driven step, a settled tank usually needs a wider inspection scope. The table below lists the methods most often used and what each one can and cannot show.

ConcernNDE methodWhat it showsLimits
Cracking at shell-to-bottom weld and lap welds in the breakover zoneVT, then MT or PTSurface-breaking cracks from strain at the bendNeeds cleaned weld surfaces, and shows only surface-breaking flaws
Soil-side floor corrosion under low areas and at the chimeFloor scanning by magnetic flux leakage with UT prove-upScreens the floor area for underside metal loss, and UT then sizes the remaining thicknessCoverage drops near the shell, at lap welds and on heavily distorted plates. Read the scanner's dead zones off the report.
Annular or critical-zone plate thicknessUT thickness and scanningRemaining thickness where the code's limits are tightestNeeds access inside the tank. Readings near the shell weld need careful probe placement.
Shell distortion near tilt or out-of-plane low pointsShell geometry survey or 3D scan, plus UT thicknessOut-of-roundness and local distortion, along with the thickness the stresses act onGeometry data supports an engineering evaluation but does not make the acceptance decision
Nozzle and piping strain from uniform settlement or tiltVT of nozzle reinforcement, supports and piping flexibility, with MT or PT of nozzle welds if distress is seenSigns of overstress where the tank connects to fixed pipingOverstress before cracking is not visible, so the piping engineer may need a stress check
Bottom welds after plate replacement or re-levelingVacuum box testing of new welds, as API 653 requires for bottom repairsLeak paths in new or repaired bottom weldsProves tightness only. It is not a volumetric weld examination.

The comparison between MFL and UT floor scanning, including probability of detection and dead zones, is covered in MFL versus UT floor scanning. Remaining-thickness rules for pitted floors are covered in tank floor pitting and minimum remaining thickness.

Who decides what

Settlement work involves several parties, and many disputes after the fact come from unclear roles. API 653 puts the owner/operator in charge of the programme, and gives the authorized inspector the inspection judgements. Settlement evaluations beyond the simple Annex B checks belong to an engineer experienced in tank settlement.

PartyResponsibility
Owner/operatorSets the survey frequency and the programme, commissions engineering evaluations, decides on repair, re-leveling or a change of operating limits, and keeps the records
API 653 authorized inspectorInspects the tank, records signs of settlement, reviews the survey and NDE results, and sets or recommends inspection intervals under the code
Tank or geotechnical engineerBreaks down the survey, runs the Annex B checks or a more rigorous analysis, projects settlement to the next inspection, and designs any foundation repair
SurveyorProvides repeatable elevation data, benchmark control and closure records
NDE contractorPerforms the weld, floor and shell examinations the scope calls for, under qualified procedures, and reports results to the authorized inspector

Atlantis works on the NDE and data side of this table. Where earlier text on this page suggests we evaluate settlement, read it within that limit: we collect and report the data, and the inspector of record and the engineer evaluate it.

The regulatory overlay in the United States and Canada

  • Pipeline breakout tanks (PHMSA). Under 49 CFR 195.432, operators inspect each in-service breakout tank at least once each calendar year, at intervals of no more than 15 months. Atmospheric and low-pressure steel aboveground breakout tanks are inspected under API Std 653, but the regulation does not allow API 653's risk-based interval provisions to be used to set inspection intervals. The edition incorporated by reference is the one that applies, so check 49 CFR 195.3.
  • SPCC facilities (EPA). 40 CFR 112.8(c)(6) requires each aboveground container to be tested or inspected for integrity on a regular schedule and whenever material repairs are made, following industry standards. Field-erected tanks are commonly managed under API 653. Shop-fabricated tanks are commonly managed under STI SP001. A settlement finding is part of the integrity record the plan must keep.
  • States and provinces. Some states add their own tank rules, and in Canada, aboveground storage tank requirements come from provincial fire codes and environmental regulations. Confirm with the authority having jurisdiction whether API 653 is referenced and which edition applies.

For how settlement surveys fit into the wider set of inspection intervals, see API 653 tank inspection intervals. For a field checklist, see the API 653 tank inspection checklist.

Common mistakes in settlement programmes

  • Doing only a shell survey on a ringwall tank where the fill inside is what is settling.
  • Comparing edge settlement with its limit as measured, with no projection, on a tank that is still moving.
  • Reporting MFL floor coverage without its dead zones, so the strip next to the shell was never scanned.
  • Evaluating settlement and floor corrosion separately when both act on the same plate.

Settlement survey questions owners ask

How does API 653 want me to handle settlement measurement frequency for a ringwall tank with about one inch of differential settlement over two cycles?

API 653 does not set a fixed frequency. It expects a planned frequency based on predicted settlement and service history. Movement of about an inch over two cycles counts as active settlement, so the owner should shorten the survey interval, track the rate at each point, and have an engineer project each settlement component to the next inspection date before comparing it with the Annex B limits.

Is a settlement survey required at every API 653 inspection?

No. A survey is required with a hydrostatic test, unless the tank's history shows acceptable settlement and none is expected. Otherwise the owner schedules surveys, and inspections should record signs of settlement for follow-up.

What instrument should be used for a tank settlement survey?

Any method accurate enough to resolve the differences being judged and repeatable from one cycle to the next. Digital levels and total stations are common, and 3D laser scanning adds shell geometry. Use the same method, benchmark and points each cycle.

What NDE is needed after a settlement finding?

Annex B calls for visual and MT or PT examination of shell-to-bottom and bottom welds once edge settlement passes a fraction of its allowable. Floor MFL with UT prove-up, and UT of the annular zone, are commonly added to check for underside corrosion in the settled area.

Does re-leveling a tank fix settlement damage?

No. Re-leveling corrects geometry but does not remove plastic strain. Overstrained plate and welds still need replacement or engineering evaluation, and the cause of the settlement needs correcting.

Do PHMSA breakout tank rules allow risk-based settlement or inspection intervals?

For breakout tanks under 49 CFR 195.432, the regulation applies API 653 but excludes its risk-based interval provisions for setting inspection intervals. Check the edition incorporated by reference.

Who signs off a settlement evaluation?

The engineer who carried out the evaluation, under the owner's programme, with the API 653 authorized inspector reviewing it for the inspection record. Surveyors and NDE contractors supply data but do not accept the tank.
